\section{Scaling predictability}
\label{app:rq01_scaling_predictability}

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}
\paragraph{Research Question.} \emph{Which benchmarks, and which per-language measurements, move with model size in a way a log-linear fit captures, so that a small-model measurement has a trend to extrapolate from at all?}

\paragraph{Setup.} We fit the final score of each task against model size with a log-linear fit, one series per task and language setting. We fit only on the sizes where the task is above chance, and we need at least three of them. We use the deep cells with the baseline data at seed 1904, 90M--1.7B. Each task is one point, the median over its language settings.
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}
\begin{rqfinding}
\textbf{Accuracy scales log-linearly where it is above chance.} 1169 gated (task, K) fits over 419 benchmark tasks, median R$^2$ 0.88 (IQR 0.77--0.94). Per-language BPB 1.00 (106 fits, 50 languages), training loss 0.98--1.00 at every K. (Figure~\ref{fig:app_rq01_scaling_predictability}.)

\textbf{The gate decides which benchmarks have a law at all.} 427 of 896 accuracy and BPB tasks are at chance wherever a fit was possible, and 17 of 42 families lose every task, among them Global-PIQA parallel (0/63), Belebele (0/59), INCLUDE (0/36) and Global-MMLU (0/29).

\textbf{A letter-answer benchmark's bBPB scales far better once reformulated.} Over the eight letter-format families the original's bBPB fits at median R$^2$ 0.53 and its \texttt{rf\_} twin's at 0.97 (530 fits each, 5--6 rungs).
\end{rqfinding}
\end{minipage}
